newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Despite strikes, Seoul subway runs on time.
newsitem.headline: Despite strikes, Seoul subway runs on time.

text.p: Non-union drivers averted chaos on Seoul's subway on Saturday, filling in for colleagues who walked out in protest at a new labour bill.

While much of South Korean industry was idled by snowballing industrial action, trains in the capital ran on time. The only inconvenience for an estimated four million passengers who use the system daily was closed ticket booths that forced passengers to use automated machines.
Bank tellers announced they would join stoppages that have shut car plants and shipyards and that threaten to stall the country's economic recovery if they drag on.
Workers at the central Bank of Korea and all other banks around the country will stage a one-day strike next Saturday in protest at a new law, a union leader said.
Hyun Ki-hwan, vice president of a bank union group, said a decision on whether to extend the action further would be made at a later date.
Starting immediately, tellers and other unionised staff would refuse to wear uniforms.
The union body, under the officially recognised Federation of Korean Trade Unions, claims to represent 132,000 workers at banks and mutual savings firms.
Bank workers feel particularly vulnerable to layoffs, authorised under the new labour law, because financial market opening is expected to spark a wave of mergers in the heavily-protected industry.
The subway strike marked a new stage in the strikes because of its impact on everyday life.
Police were posted at stations to prevent union members from disrupting the service.

"I only waited one minute," said Kim Yoon-hwe, 24, on his way to work. Most Koreans still work a half day on Saturday. "I haven't felt inconvenienced by the strikes. But I'm sure I will if they go on."
Strikes began on Thursday after the government rammed through the labour law in a clandestine dawn session of the National Assembly.

Lee Hong-koo, chairman of the ruling New Korea Party, called a news conference to try to resolve "misunderstanding" Koreans have about the labour legislation, which also allows companies to introduce flexible working hours and replace strikers.
"We revised the law to protect workers rights and give management the flexibility it needs to maintain competitiveness," Lee said.
"The goal and reason behind the new law seem to be misunderstood by the people."
